extracted.intended_audience: media studies students, journalism scholars, journalism researchers, and anyone studying newsroom production or news-values
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply operational newsroom constraints (time, logistics, format, professional ideology, sources) as determinants of newsworthiness, with emphasis on television/BBC newsroom practices in the 1970s. Useful for analyzing how outlet-side capacities shape story selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Stop-Watch Culture (Time-Slavery)
rubrics_metrics.description: News production is organized around clock-deadlines; events that fit newsroom deadlines attain newsworthiness while events on incompatible timescales are demoted or deferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines structure what can be covered and how stories are packaged; schedule compatibility increases selection probability. Antipattern: treating importance of an event as independent from whether it can meet immediate bulletin timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics / Resource Deployability
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is newsworthy if a crew or reporter can be physically dispatched in time; geographic concentration of staff biases coverage toward accessible events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource constraints (reporter availability, crew, transport) function as gating conditions. Stories requiring inaccessible or scarce resources are less likely to be covered regardless of event significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must fit broadcast formats (e.g., 90 seconds, 2-minute package); stories that cannot be compressed into available formats lose news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format limits shape what aspects of events are selected and how they're told. Editors favor events that can be told within existing slot lengths and package structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulletin Slot Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed bulletin slots (lead, second story, regional, sports, weather) shape story selection by slot availability and expected function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The architecture of the program (which slots exist and their purposes) exerts demand-pull on what stories are sought and how they are ranked. Selection is partly a function of fitting a story to a specific slot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture/Visuals Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: For television, lack of usable pictures reduces news value; visual availability can outweigh importance in editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television prioritizes events that yield strong visuals. Important but visually thin stories may be downgraded or omitted. Antipattern: overvaluing ’important’ events without considering visual practicability for TV.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Imperative of "Coverage"
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must fill the bulletin every day, creating demand-pull that can lower thresholds for what is considered news when supply is short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The routine need to populate programs leads to treating some stories as newsworthy primarily because slots must be filled, not solely because of inherent event newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional Self-Image
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters internalize the BBC's ethos (e.g., impartiality, responsible journalism), which filters out stories that would compromise those professional values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational ideology and professional identity act as selection filters — stories incompatible with institutional norms (e.g., two-sided framing for impartiality) are demoted even if eventful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire-Service Dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC depended heavily on wire services (e.g., Reuters, PA) for international news, importing wire-service news values into editorial selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on external wire feeds biases coverage toward events prioritized by those services and shapes what international stories reach the newsroom.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Hierarchy of Credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials and establishment sources are accorded automatic credibility; alternative or non-establishment sources must establish theirs to be treated as credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source hierarchies influence story selection and framing; stories backed by high-credibility sources are easier to run. Editors avoid sources that would require additional verification or risk credibility challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Avoidance of Trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors avoid stories that risk libel, official complaint, or audience backlash; newsworthiness includes a defensibility component alongside event properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk-management considerations (legal, political, reputational) constrain selection. Antipattern: selecting controversial items without accounting for institutional risk tolerances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Pure News-Values Approaches (Production-Side Constraints Matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract lists of news-values (e.g., Galtung & Ruge) understate the role of production-side constraints; the same event will be evaluated differently depending on outlet resources, format, and routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of newsworthiness must incorporate outlet-side variables (resources, beats, format, deadlines, professional ideology). Comparative analyses should account for how wire-rich, beat-rich, or resource-stretched newsrooms will differently select and frame identical events.
